prompt:
Data Stream Processing Systems (DSPS):
a) What is the motivation for data stream processing systems?
b) Which applications typically use DSPS?
hints: Ask what happens to the usefulness of a data item as time passes.
Think about whether storing the whole stream first is even possible.
Name application areas where a reaction hours later is worthless.
keyPoints: Stream data is unbounded - it never stops arriving, so it cannot all be stored
The value of data decays fast: results are needed in (near) real time, while the data is still relevant
Store-then-query gives too high latency and may exceed feasible storage
DSPS process data in motion: standing queries are registered once and run continuously as events arrive
Applications: sensor/IoT monitoring, finance (fraud detection, trading), network and traffic monitoring, log and clickstream analysis
modelAnswer: The motivation is that many data sources never stop producing data, and the value of the data drops fast with time. A traditional database assumes you store the data first and run queries afterwards. For an unbounded stream - sensor readings, stock ticks, network packets, server logs - storing everything first is often impossible or pointless: by the time you could query it, the moment to react has passed. A DSPS turns the model around: queries are registered once and run continuously, and every new event is processed as it arrives, typically kept only in small windows. Typical applications: monitoring and alerting over sensor or IoT data, fraud detection and algorithmic trading in finance, network intrusion and traffic monitoring, and real-time analytics on clickstreams or logs. What these share is that the answer must be ready seconds after the event, and the old raw data is rarely queried again.
followUps: Which of these applications could tolerate being 10 minutes late, and which could not?
Where does a DSPS keep the data it has already seen?

prompt: What are the main differences between a traditional database system (DBS) and a data stream processing system (DSPS)?
hints: In which of the two systems is the data persistent, and in which is the query persistent?
How many times can a query look at the same data item in each system?
Consider what operators like a full sort or a full join need in order to finish.
keyPoints: DBS: data at rest, finite and persisted; DSPS: data in motion, unbounded, mostly transient
DBS: one-shot queries that can re-read data arbitrarily; DSPS: continuous standing queries, one pass over each event
Roles are reversed: in a DBS the data is stored and queries come and go; in a DSPS queries are stored and data flows through
Finite memory means DSPS work on windows/synopses; blocking operators (full sort, full join) are problematic
DSPS may answer approximately; a DBS answers exactly over stored state
Both share the relational foundation: selection, projection, aggregation and joins exist in both
modelAnswer: In a traditional DBS the data is at rest: it is stored once, and queries arrive, run to completion over the stored data, and can read the same rows as often as they like. In a DSPS the data is in motion: each event is seen once and then typically discarded, while queries are registered up front and run continuously - the roles of data and queries are swapped. Because memory is finite and the stream is unbounded, a DSPS cannot keep everything; it evaluates over windows or synopses of recent data, and blocking operators like a full sort are a problem since they want to see the end of the data. Answers may therefore be approximate. Latency is the other big difference: a DSPS produces results while events arrive, in milliseconds to seconds, whereas a DBS answers only after the data has been stored and a query is submitted. The shared part is the relational toolbox: select, project, aggregate and join appear in both, but with different assumptions underneath.
followUps: Why is 'sort the whole stream' an impossible query, and what could you sort instead?
Which consistency and recovery guarantees of a DBS are hard to keep in a DSPS?

prompt:
a) What is a window in a data stream processing system?
b) What are windows used for?
hints: A stream is infinite but memory is not - what can a system actually keep?
Think about when a question like 'the average so far' stops being useful.
Recall how the Esper assignment restricted queries to recent days.
keyPoints: A window is a bounded portion of the unbounded stream - e.g. the last N events or the last T time units
Windows exist because memory is finite: only a finite part of an infinite stream can be kept
Recent data is usually what matters; old data loses relevance
Windows make aggregation over streams well defined: 'average over the last 7 days' needs a finite portion
Windows are defined by count or by time, and come as sliding or tumbling
modelAnswer: A window is a bounded portion of a stream: either the most recent N events, or the events of the last T time units, or a batch that opens and closes on some boundary. Its purpose follows from two hard facts about streams. First, the stream is unbounded but memory is not, so we can only ever keep a finite part of it. Second, for most questions only recent data matters - a monitoring system reacts to what happened in the last minutes, not the whole history. Windows also make aggregation over a stream meaningful: 'the average temperature of the last 7 days' is well defined over a window, while an 'average of everything so far' grows forever and says less and less about now. So windows are the unit that stream queries are evaluated on, and they come in two main shapes - sliding windows that advance continuously, and tumbling windows that move in fixed batches - like the #length(7) and #length_batch(7) views in the Esper assignment.
followUps: How would you answer a question about data that has already fallen out of the window?
What is the difference between a count-based and a time-based window for irregular arrival rates?

prompt:
a) Compare tumbling and sliding windows.
b) What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?
hints: Ask: can one event ever belong to two windows at the same time?
Think about a pattern that starts at the end of one window - what happens to it at a window boundary?
In the Esper assignment, both shapes existed: which view released a result only every 7th day?
keyPoints: Tumbling: fixed, non-overlapping batches; each event in exactly one window; window empties between batches
Sliding: window advances on every new event (or time tick); windows overlap; an event can be in several windows
Tumbling advantages: simple, at most one output per batch, clean 'per week' semantics
Tumbling disadvantages: boundary effects (patterns crossing the edge are cut in two) and late results (nothing until the batch closes)
Sliding advantages: always reflects the newest data, detects things sooner
Sliding disadvantages: more computation and memory traffic per event, overlapping/repeated outputs for the same period
modelAnswer: A tumbling window is a sequence of fixed, non-overlapping batches: it collects events until it is full - say 7 tuples - releases them as one batch, empties, and starts over. Every event belongs to exactly one window, and the system produces at most one result per batch. That makes tumbling windows simple and predictable, which suits reports like weekly totals. The disadvantages are boundary effects: a pattern that crosses a batch boundary, like a heat wave spanning the end of one week and the start of the next, is cut in two and may be missed; and results arrive late, since nothing is reported until the batch closes. A sliding window keeps the most recent N events - or the last T time units - and re-evaluates on every arrival, so windows overlap and each event sits in several of them. It always reflects the newest data and detects things sooner, but it does more work per event and can output many overlapping results for what is essentially the same period. In Esper terms: #length_batch(7) versus #length(7).
followUps: For the 7-day average above 82 from the Esper assignment, which window would you choose and why?
How many results does the sliding version produce per arriving day, once the window is full?
